name: Chechnya
summary:
Chechnya operates outside the Russian federal legal framework in practice. In February 2017, Chechen law-enforcement and security officials launched an anti-gay purge, rounding up dozens of men, holding them in unofficial detention facilities (documented by name and location, including a secret prison in Argun), humiliating, starving, and torturing them, forcibly disappearing some, and returning others to families "barely alive from beatings" after captors exposed them and encouraged relatives to carry out honour killings (HRW, 2017). Novaya Gazeta reported in January 2019 that persecution had resumed and the Argun facility was "full again," while Kadyrov's press chief publicly denied any unofficial detention sites exist.

The pattern has mutated and continues: North Caucasus SOS documented at least seven cases of Chechen security forces blackmailing detained homosexual men into "volunteering" for front-line conscription in Ukraine (one already killed), and Memorial found a mass wave of unlawful detentions tied to forced conscription. In 2021, Kadyrov's aide announced the abduction of two men evacuated abroad, taken at the Gudermes police station. The UK Home Office CPIN (June 2025) explicitly names the North Caucasus as the exception to its finding of no state-persecution risk elsewhere in Russia.

For a visitor discovered or outed, the evidence indicates near-certain detention without legal process, torture, coerced conscription or death, with no functioning judicial remedy. This is approximately 0.11 below the national score of 0.12, reflecting a governance system where the state's security apparatus operates outside all legal constraint. Far below every other unit in the federation; even Dagestan and Ingushetia (0.04), which share the North Caucasus security logic, lack Chechnya's documented scale of extrajudicial killing and secret-prison infrastructure.

name: Dagestan
summary:
Dagestan falls within the North Caucasus regional exception identified by the UK Home Office CPIN (June 2025) and named in Canadian and Australian travel advisories as part of a distinct don't-travel zone. Canada specifically warns that visitors must obtain special permission from the Ministry of the Interior to enter certain areas. North Caucasus SOS's David Isteev states flatly that "there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families," adding that "every year it gets worse."

No separate Dagestan-specific written law or documented Chechnya-style purge exists, but the republic shares the same security-and-custom enforcement logic: the federal transition ban and propaganda law operate in a context where local security structures and family honour norms produce extrajudicial responses unmediated by legal process, and where special-access restrictions impede independent monitoring and foreign consular support. This places Dagestan approximately 0.08 below the national score of 0.12. Well below the oblasts of central Russia (which sit at national) due to the regional-exception designation; above Chechnya (0.01), whose documented secret-prison and killing infrastructure has no confirmed equivalent in Dagestan.

name: Ingushetia
summary:
Ingushetia is one of the republics explicitly named in the Canadian travel advisory's special-permission requirement (alongside Chechnya and Dagestan) and falls within the North Caucasus zone that the UK Home Office CPIN (June 2025) identifies as the exception to its finding of no state-persecution risk in Russia generally. Isteev of North Caucasus SOS states there is "no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus," where private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families.

Like Dagestan, Ingushetia shares the security-and-custom enforcement logic without a documented Chechnya-scale purge infrastructure. The special-access regime limits independent monitoring and foreign consular intervention. Score approximately 0.08 below national (0.12). Equal to Dagestan in evidence quality; well above Chechnya (0.01), which has confirmed secret prisons and extrajudicial killings absent here.

name: Kabardino-Balkaria
summary:
Kabardino-Balkaria is named within the broader North Caucasus risk zone identified by the UK Home Office CPIN (June 2025) and Western travel advisories. North Caucasus SOS's assessment that there is "no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus" encompasses this republic. The local security-and-custom enforcement logic—where family honour norms and informal security structures can produce violence, detention, or forced return to families—applies, even absent a specific documented purge infrastructure.

Unlike Chechnya, Dagestan, and Ingushetia, no separate special-permission entry requirement is specifically named for Kabardino-Balkaria in the Canadian advisory, and no Chechnya-scale extrajudicial detention site has been documented here. The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.07 below. Slightly above Dagestan/Ingushetia (0.04) to reflect the absence of the explicit special-access regime; well below the central-Russian oblasts, which sit at national.

name: Karachay-Cherkessia
summary:
Karachay-Cherkessia falls within the North Caucasus regional exception identified by the UK Home Office CPIN (June 2025) and named in Western don't-travel guidance for the Caucasus zone. The North Caucasus SOS assessment of no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the region applies here. The security-and-custom enforcement logic—informal detention, family exposure, violence unmediated by legal process—is the operative risk for a discovered visitor.

No Chechnya-style documented purge infrastructure or specific special-permission entry regime is identified for Karachay-Cherkessia. Approximately 0.07 below the national score of 0.12. Equal to Kabardino-Balkaria and North Ossetia in the broader North Caucasus bloc; above Dagestan and Ingushetia (0.04), which carry the explicit special-access designation.

name: North Ossetia–Alania
summary:
North Ossetia–Alania is included in the North Caucasus zone that the UK Home Office CPIN (June 2025) singles out as the exception to its general finding of no state-persecution risk in Russia. Western travel advisories name the republic within the broader Caucasus don't-travel area. The enforcement logic is the same as neighbouring republics: family honour norms and informal security structures can produce violence, detention, or forced return without legal process.

No Chechnya-scale secret-prison infrastructure or explicit special-permission entry requirement is documented for North Ossetia specifically. Approximately 0.07 below national (0.12). Equal to Kabardino-Balkaria and Karachay-Cherkessia in the broader North Caucasus bloc. Well above the central-Russian oblasts, which inherit the national score with no sub-national deviation.

name: Stavropol Krai
summary:
Stavropol Krai is named in the Canadian travel advisory's special-permission requirement (alongside Chechnya, Dagestan, and Ingushetia) and is included in the North Caucasus zone identified by the UK Home Office CPIN as the exception to Russia's general risk picture. The dossier specifically identifies the south-eastern part bordering Chechnya as subject to the same security-and-custom enforcement logic. However, Stavropol is a krai, not a republic, and the extreme documented violence (secret prisons, purges, coerced conscription) is Chechen-specific rather than krai-wide.

For a visitor, the special-permission regime itself restricts movement and independent oversight, and the south-eastern areas adjacent to Chechnya share the localised security culture. The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.05 below. Above the core North Caucasus republics (Dagestan, Ingushetia at 0.04; Kabardino-Balkaria, Karachay-Cherkessia, North Ossetia at 0.05) because the extreme evidence is geographically limited to the Chechnya border zone within a large multi-ethnic krai, and no independent republic-level security apparatus analogous to Kadyrov's exists.

name: Moscow
summary:
Moscow concentrates enforcement activity of the federal anti-LGBT framework: club raids, the arrest of Kotov as the first person charged with *creating* an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds (late December 2024), and the medical and bureaucratic gatekeeping that the 2023 federal transition ban imposes. The Moscow Times' 2025 survey of persecution is titled around "arrests, club raids and extremism charges." A foreign visitor encountering Moscow police faces the federal propaganda-law penalty—up to 15 days' detention and deportation—applied in a jurisdiction with the highest police density and most active venue-level enforcement in the country.

The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.03 below. The severity of the law is identical everywhere (it is federal), but Moscow's role as the primary venue for enforcement operations and its concentration of bureaucratic touchpoints (document verification, medical access, hotel registration) materially raise a visitor's probability of encountering active application. Comparable to Orenburg Oblast (0.09), which produced the country's first criminal extremism conviction against a commercial venue; both represent enforcement-active jurisdictions within the uniform federal framework.

name: Orenburg Oblast
summary:
Orenburg Oblast is the jurisdiction where the federal "LGBT extremism" designation first produced a criminal conviction against a commercial leisure venue. The Pose bar case (submitted to court July 2025 by the regional Investigative Committee) resulted in June 2026 in a seven-year sentence for owner Vyacheslav Khasanov, prison terms for two employees, and forfeiture of over one million rubles—Russia's first criminal LGBT-extremism sentencing. The precedent establishes that a bar or club can be prosecuted as an extremist organisation, which is the scenario a foreign visitor walking into a commercial venue is most likely to encounter.

This is visitor-facing enforcement: the venue context (drinking, socialising) is exactly where a visiting trans person might interact with the criminal justice system. The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.03 below. Comparable to Moscow (0.09), which concentrates raids and the first organiser prosecution; both represent active enforcement venues within the uniform federal law. Orenburg's specific finding—a seven-year sentence against a bar owner—sets the most severe commercial-venue precedent in the country.
